question: Which AI regulatory instrument best reduces expected harm from frontier AI over the next five years, keeping the technology sector's net loss below $400bn and the gross social cost under $150bn?

policies.label: Status quo (voluntary commitments)
policies.note: No new obligation. Existing consumer and product law only, with the regulator's present capacity. Every other policy is measured against this path, pair by pair.
policies.name: baseline

policies.label: Transparency and disclosure
policies.note: Model documentation, provenance marking and public incident disclosure. Cheap, and it shrinks the misuse environment rather than the capability.
policies.name: transparency_disclosure

policies.label: Compute threshold reporting
policies.note: Developers above a training compute threshold report their models and their own evaluations. The regime an executive order can create.
policies.name: compute_threshold_reporting

policies.label: Mandatory third party evaluation
policies.note: Independent pre deployment evaluation above a threshold, with a short approval delay. Catches a share of unsafe releases before they ship.
policies.name: mandatory_third_party_evals

policies.label: Risk tiering (EU style)
policies.note: Obligations by use case tier for every deployer, conformity assessment before high risk deployment, a sandbox for small firms. Compliance cost scales with deployment, not with the frontier.
policies.name: risk_tiering

policies.label: Frontier licensing
policies.note: A licence to train or deploy above the capability threshold: mandated safety spend, independent evaluation, an approval delay, audits with real fines. Domestic scope: a mobile lab can leave.
policies.name: frontier_licensing

policies.label: Strict liability
policies.note: Firms pay for the harm their systems cause, insured by mandate. No ex ante obligation: the price of an incident does the work, and the firms choose their own safety spend.
policies.name: strict_liability

policies.label: Liability with a safe harbour
policies.note: Strict liability, but a firm that meets the evaluation and safety spend standard is shielded from most of it. Compliance becomes the cheaper choice.
policies.name: liability_with_safe_harbour

policies.label: Six month moratorium above the threshold
policies.note: Releases above the capability threshold are frozen for six months, then reporting applies. The sharpest brake and the one most easily left behind.
policies.name: moratorium

benchmarks.title: Annual growth of recorded AI incidents

observations.label: AI Incident Database, 2023 to 2024
AI Incident Database, 2024 to 2025 (233 to 362)

benchmarks.se_basis: Poisson error of the annual counts (about 149, 233 and 362)
benchmarks.transport_basis: the database is compiled from media reports and its curators attribute an unknown share of the rise to reporting and attention; the model counts incidents at eight firm archetypes, not in the whole economy

sources.cite: Stanford HAI, AI Index Report 2025, chapter 3 (233 incidents in 2024, up 56.4% on 2023)
Stanford HAI, AI Index Report 2026, responsible AI (362 incidents in 2025)

benchmarks.mapping: the status quo's expected number of incidents in each year of the horizon; the benchmark is compared with the average annual growth of that count
benchmarks.caveat: growth in recorded incidents is joint growth in harms, deployment and attention

benchmarks.title: Annual change in public trust in AI and AI companies

observations.label: Edelman, trust in AI companies, 28 country average, 61% to 53% over five years
Edelman, trust in AI companies, United States, 50% to 35% over five years
Pew, US adults not more concerned than excited about AI, 63% (2021) to 50% (2025)

benchmarks.se_basis: standard deviation of the three series over root three
benchmarks.transport_basis: a survey share is compared with the model's trust index, which starts at one and has no survey counterpart

sources.cite: Edelman Trust Barometer 2024, key insights around AI
Pew Research Center, How Americans view AI and its impact on people and society, September 2025

benchmarks.mapping: the status quo's trust index at the end of the horizon, as an annual relative change from its starting value
benchmarks.caveat: the period measured had no AI specific regulation in most of the countries surveyed, which is what the status quo represents; the fall may have causes other than harm

benchmarks.title: Share of a fall in trust recovered about nine months after a salient incident

observations.label: AAA: afraid to ride in a self driving vehicle, 63% before the 2018 crashes, 73% after, 71% in January 2019

benchmarks.se_basis: each survey has a margin of error of four points at 95% (about 1,000 interviews); delta method on the ratio
benchmarks.transport_basis: another technology, and fear of using it is not trust in the firms that build it; the interval between the two surveys is known to within a few months

sources.cite: AAA, Three in four Americans remain afraid of fully self driving vehicles, March 2019
Smart Cities Dive, AAA poll, March 2019 (the 2018 figure and the crashes)

benchmarks.mapping: with monthly recovery r and no further incident, the share of a fall recovered after nine months is 1 - (1 - r)^9

benchmarks.title: Compliance cost of a high risk regime as a share of development spending in scope

observations.label: European Commission impact assessment: roughly 4 to 5% of a EUR 170,000 system
Supporting study (Renda et al.): about 17% with external services and staff

benchmarks.se_basis: standard deviation of the two ex ante estimates over root two
benchmarks.transport_basis: an ex ante estimate per system built from a standard cost model, which its authors call a theoretical maximum; the model's cost is an instrument parameter applied to revenue in scope

sources.cite: European Commission, SWD(2021) 84 final, impact assessment of the AI Act
Renda et al. (2021), Study to support an impact assessment of regulatory requirements for AI in Europe

benchmarks.mapping: under risk tiering, compliance spending over the R&D spending of the firms in scope on the activity in scope, while in force
benchmarks.caveat: the share of systems that are high risk was never estimated by any party to the assessment

benchmarks.title: Effect of a horizontal compliance regime on the profits of firms in scope

observations.label: GDPR, exposed firms in 61 countries: profits down about 8% (Chen, Frey and Presidente)
GDPR, data intensive EU sectors: profit margin down 1.9% (Koski and Valmari)
GDPR, large technology firms: no significant effect (Chen, Frey and Presidente)

benchmarks.se_basis: standard deviation of the three estimates over root three
benchmarks.transport_basis: data protection, not AI; a broad cross section of firms against eight archetypes that are mostly large

sources.cite: Chen, Frey and Presidente (2022), Privacy regulation and firm performance, Oxford Martin working paper 2022-1
Johnson (2022), Economic research on privacy regulation: lessons from the GDPR and beyond, NBER working paper 30705

benchmarks.mapping: under risk tiering, the industry's earnings against the status quo on the same paths, over the months in force
benchmarks.caveat: the estimates differ in sample, outcome and period; the mean of three is a summary, not a pooled estimate

benchmarks.title: Equity return when a horizontal regime becomes enforceable

observations.label: GDPR, 1,013 US firms, week of enforcement: lower bound
GDPR, 1,013 US firms, week of enforcement: upper bound

benchmarks.transport_basis: a week against the model's month; most of the cost of a law announced years earlier is in the price before it applies

sources.cite: Motoki and Pinto (2024), Journal of Business Finance and Accounting (press summary)

benchmarks.mapping: under risk tiering, the value weighted index's change in the month the instrument takes effect, less the status quo's on the same path
benchmarks.caveat: the enforcement date return understates the total cost capitalised

benchmarks.title: Equity return of a firm when a regulatory fine is announced

observations.label: GDPR fines, 25 announcements, window (0,1)
window (0,2)
window (0,3)
window (0,4)

benchmarks.se_basis: the published t statistics (about 3 on estimates of about 0.007)
benchmarks.transport_basis: data protection fines, most of them small against the firm's size; days against the model's month

sources.cite: Ford et al. (2021), The impact of GDPR infringement fines on the market value of firms, ECCWS

benchmarks.mapping: under risk tiering, a fined firm's log return in the month of the fine less the index's
benchmarks.caveat: 25 announcements; windows beyond five days are not significant in the source

benchmarks.title: Equity return of a firm when a serious incident becomes public

observations.label: Cyberattacks with loss of personal financial information, 2005 to 2014, three day window

benchmarks.se_basis: an allowance: the standard error was not in the summary consulted
benchmarks.transport_basis: data breaches, not AI incidents; three days against the model's month

sources.cite: Kamiya, Kang, Kim, Milidonis and Stulz, What is the impact of successful cyberattacks on target firms? (authors' summary, Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, March 2018; Journal of Financial Economics 139(3), 2021)

benchmarks.mapping: under the status quo, the log return of a firm in a month with a major incident at that firm, less the index's
benchmarks.caveat: the model's major incident is defined by monetised harm, a breach by the data lost

benchmarks.title: Share of regulated activity displaced abroad by a unilateral regime

observations.label: Carbon leakage ratio without border adjustment, 25 studies, 310 estimates: mean

benchmarks.se_basis: a quarter of the published range (5% to 25%)
benchmarks.transport_basis: carbon pricing, and mostly ex ante models; AI activity is divisible in some respects (where a model is trained) and not in others (one set of weights)
benchmarks.mapping: under frontier licensing, the revenue of the firms in scope booked offshore in the last year of the horizon, as a share of their revenue
benchmarks.caveat: for AI regulation leakage is theorised, surveyed and anecdotal, not measured

benchmarks.title: Premium above expected claims in liability insurance

observations.label: US property and casualty industry 2023: premiums over losses and loss expenses (76.2%), less one

benchmarks.se_basis: two years of an industry aggregate
benchmarks.transport_basis: all property and casualty lines; cover for AI liability is not an established line

sources.cite: NAIC, U.S. property and casualty and title insurance industries, 2023 full year results

benchmarks.mapping: the assumption itself: the premium charged above the expected liability under a mandate
benchmarks.caveat: an industry average over lines with very different tails

benchmarks.title: Share of the insurance loading used up by underwriting and administration

observations.label: US property and casualty industry 2023: expense ratio 24.9% over premiums less losses and loss expenses (23.8%)

benchmarks.se_basis: two years of an industry aggregate
benchmarks.transport_basis: all property and casualty lines, in two years with an underwriting loss (the share is above one because expenses exceeded the loading)

sources.cite: NAIC, U.S. property and casualty and title insurance industries, 2023 full year results

benchmarks.mapping: the assumption itself: the share of the loading that is a real resource cost and not a transfer to insurers
benchmarks.caveat: the model's range (0.25 to 0.75) treats part of the loading as insurers' margin; in these two years there was none
